transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-09-15 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Daniel Chu (Redwood SE), Rae Kim (Redwood Product) -- Maya Rivera (CTO, Orion), Liam O'Connor (ML Lead), Priya Singh (Infra), Jason Park (Data Scientist)

Summary: Walkthrough of Optimize quantization profiles — focused on INT8 vs FP8, examples of quality vs latency tradeoffs, and what we'd run during a pilot. Customer asked about privacy/VPC and regression detection.

[00:00] Sofia Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. we thought we'd walk through the Optimize quant profiles and show some of the numbers we've been seeing across int8 and fp8 on typical summarization and qa workloads.
[00:18] Maya Rivera: Thanks Sofia. We're mostly interested in anything that gets us under 150ms p95 on short prompts without losing answer quality. Our current stack is mixed: some hosted endpoints and a few on-prem GPUs.
[00:30] Daniel Chu: Cool, thanks Maya. quick note, we'll show the profiling and then talk pilot scope — we usually compare INT8 and FP8 profiles, show quality deltas with our eval harness, and then show latency numbers at different batch sizes.
[00:45] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. We care about hallucinations and factuality. If we drop to int8, what's the typical hit on QA accuracy?
[01:05] Daniel Chu: Yeah, good question. generally on our benchmarks int8 gives you like a 1-3% drop on closed-book QA F1 depending on model family and prompt style; fp8 is usually much closer to fp16 — sub 0.5% delta. but those are rough numbers, we should run on your prompts. also model architecture matters — decoder-only vs encoder-decoder behave a little different.
[01:35] Jason Park: when you say int8, do you mean per-channel symmetric quant or the mixed scheme?
[01:45] Rae Kim: We typically use a per-channel asymmetric calibration with a mixed-int8 path for certain ops, and we choose kernel variants per-layer. there is some heuristics in Optimize that choose which layers to keep in higher precision if quality would drop.
[02:05] Priya Singh: On the infra side, if we do a private pilot we'd need a VPC option and KMS for keys. Is that supported for the pilot or only for Private deployments?
[02:18] Sofia Patel: We can do customer-managed VPC for pilots — the private control plane option is the more full-featured private deployment but for a pilot we can set up a VPC-connected cluster with KMS integration. We'll send the security appendix after the call.
[02:35] Maya Rivera: great. also curious about cost. if fp8 is near fp16 in quality, is it also near fp16 in cost? like does fp8 give us big savings?
[02:50] Daniel Chu: fp8 tends to be a win on both cost and latency on newer hardware that supports fp8 kernels — there are fewer memory and bandwidth savings than int8, but runtime is often faster per-token because of smaller data movement. int8 gives larger memory savings, which lets you fit larger batches and sometimes reduces tail latency but with slightly more quality risk.
[03:20] Liam O'Connor: can you show an example chart?
[03:28] Daniel Chu: sure, let me pull up the Optimize dashboard. 
[03:35] [screen share noise] 
[03:40] Daniel Chu: ok on screen — here is a quality vs latency chart. x-axis is p95 latency, y-axis is Rouge-F1 for summarization test set. blue is fp16 baseline, orange is fp8 profile, green is int8. you can see fp8 clusters very close to fp16 but shifts slightly left (lower latency). int8 sits further left (lower latency) but there's a small drop in quality on some prompts.
[04:10] Maya Rivera: that pattern matches what we've seen. do you have per-prompt deltas? some prompts are more sensitive.
[04:22] Daniel Chu: yes we produce prompt-level diffs in the eval harness so you can see which prompt families degrade. part of Optimize is the regression alerting tied to your prompt sets — if certain prompts cross a threshold we flag them.
[04:40] Jason Park: how do you handle cache / kv cache with quantized models — does it affect correctness?
[04:50] Rae Kim: KV cache is precision-agnostic at the API level — we maintain logical token keys and the runtime handles the numeric representation. occasionally when you aggressively quantize some layers it changes activation distributions and you can see small generation differences, but not corruption. we've got heuristics to keep critical attention kernels in higher precision.
[05:15] Maya Rivera: for our use case we do a lot of short-turn QA where latency is king. p95 under 150ms is a target, but we also need 99th under 250ms. Are those feasible with int8 on your Dedicated clusters?
[05:30] Daniel Chu: On dedicated pools with the right GPUs (A100X or H100-class) and optimized kernels, int8 p95 under 150ms on short prompts is doable with small batch sizes and KV caching. 99th under 250ms is more sensitive to load and batching patterns — we'll need to benchmark with your real traffic shape.
[06:00] Liam O'Connor: what's the turnaround for a pilot benchmark?
[06:07] Sofia Patel: we typically do a 1-week focused benchmark: day 0 onboarding and data/requirements, day 1 run baseline on fp16, day 2-3 run fp8/int8 profiles and analyze prompt-level regressions, day 4-5 tune batching and autoscale, day 6 present results. so about 7 business days.
[06:30] Priya Singh: network egress for hosted would be a concern — if we run pilot on Redwood hosted, how's data retained?
[06:40] Rae Kim: for hosted we have configurable retention policies — short-term logs for debugging, and then we can enable no-persist mode for inputs and outputs. For enterprise pilots we usually use VPC or dedicated where logs can be routed to customer's SIEM.
[06:58] Maya Rivera: ok. can you walk through one concrete example with numbers? maybe a summarization prompt with tokens and latency 
[07:08] Daniel Chu: yeah — here's a sample. prompt ~120 tokens, generation ~80 tokens. fp16 p95 220ms on this hardware at batch=2, fp8 p95 180ms, int8 p95 140ms. Quality measured by Rouge-L: fp16 0.78, fp8 0.77, int8 0.74. So int8 gives 36% lower latency in this slice but 4pts Rouge-L drop.
[07:45] Jason Park: that's bigger than we'd accept on some intents. is there a way to do hybrid routing where certain calls go to fp16 and others to int8?
[07:55] Sofia Patel: absolutely — Smart routing in the platform can route by policy: latency-critical routes to int8/low-cost variants, quality-critical to fp16/fp8. You can also do per-route thresholding or A/B rollouts.
[08:15] Liam O'Connor: how easy is it to specify those rules? via Console or API?
[08:20] Rae Kim: both. Console gives templates and a visual slider for tradeoffs; API has a policy DSL for more complex logic including headers, weights, and traffic splits.
[08:35] Maya Rivera: about regression detection — you mentioned alerting. how noisy is it in practice? we don't want 100 false alarms.
[08:45] Daniel Chu: good point. we tune alert thresholds with you and use significance testing across prompt families. you can group prompts and set minimum effect sizes — we also surface sample outputs so you can triage quickly.
[09:05] Priya Singh: from the infra side, if we use your dedicated option, do we still get the same optimize features and automatic quant profile suggestions?
[09:15] Sofia Patel: yes — Optimize is part of the platform across hosted, dedicated, and private. we ship the same profiling agent and the runtime picks kernel variants per deployment. The main differences are isolation and autoscaling controls.
[09:35] Liam O'Connor: any known issues with certain model families when going int8? e.g., instruction-tuned chat models?
[09:45] Rae Kim: instruction-tuned and RLHF models can be a bit more sensitive — especially on multi-turn chat. for those we often keep the first few attention layers at higher precision or prefer fp8. We also provide per-layer recommendations in the quant profile.
[10:10] Maya Rivera: what about eval metrics beyond Rouge — we use factuality and hallucination checks too.
[10:18] Daniel Chu: we can plug in your eval suites; Optimize accepts multiple metrics and will compute tradeoff curves per metric so you can pick a profile that meets your factuality threshold.
[10:30] Jason Park: we have a proprietary hallucination classifier — can that be used in the tuning loop?
[10:35] Rae Kim: yes, you can integrate your classifier to produce a metric and we run optimization against that. we just need the output in the harness format.
[10:50] Sofia Patel: quick pause — any other questions before I show the pilot template?
[10:55] Maya Rivera: no, please go ahead.
[11:00] Sofia Patel: Alright pilot template. we include: required assets, sample prompt set, latency SLOs, VPC info, success criteria (p95/99 latency, quality threshold, cost target). we also include a quick benchmark script you can run locally or we can run it for you.
[11:25] Liam O'Connor: on the sample set — we'll share a mix of short QA and long-form summarization. Is 500 prompts enough?
[11:35] Daniel Chu: 500 is a great start, split across intent buckets. we recommend 200 short QA, 200 medium summarization, 100 long context to cover tails.
[11:45] Priya Singh: for VPC peering, what ports and egress rules do you need?
[11:52] Rae Kim: We'll send a short checklist — primarily outbound to our control plane on TLS 443, and then internal annotations for the compute fleet. We'll include firewall examples.
[12:05] Maya Rivera: can you put a rough price range for pilot + a 3-month dedicated commit?
[12:12] Sofia Patel: rough estimate: pilot is low-cost — typically a few thousand dollars depending on scale (mostly compute). For a 3-month dedicated commit we'd size GPU hours and provide a commit discount — I'll include ranges in the pricing doc.
[12:28] Jason Park: any compliance certifications relevant? We handle regulated data so SOC2 and ISO are the big ones.
[12:34] Rae Kim: we are SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 compliant; we'll attach the certs and the security appendix. For private/on-prem we can support air-gapped deployments off the control plane if needed.
[12:50] Liam O'Connor: curious about monitoring — token-level cost breakdown you mentioned earlier — is that per-route?
[12:58] Rae Kim: yes, Console shows token breakdowns per route/model, latency percentiles, and you can break down by API key, tenant, or route. we also have traced generation logs for debugging.
[13:15] Maya Rivera: ok this is helpful. next steps I think — we'll share prompts, you'll share configs and pricing, and then we kick off the pilot.
[13:25] Sofia Patel: Perfect. I'll follow up with the quant profiles doc, security appendix, and the benchmark spreadsheet. Daniel will draft the pilot plan.
[13:35] Liam O'Connor: thanks everyone.
[13:40] Sofia Patel: Thanks all, we'll send notes and action items.

Post-call notes: Customer is interested in a pilot focused on latency-critical QA with strict p95/p99 SLOs. They leaned conservative on quality and prefer fp8 preference for chat; int8 considered only for non-critical low-latency routes. Next immediate ask: sample prompts and pricing + security docs.

End of transcript.
